title: Deepening (Learning) Understanding - 2
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton continues his account of understanding by running it through the same eight criteria he used to distinguish knowledge and skills. Understanding, he says, is not true in the conventional sense, because it is each person's own up-to-now product of simmering knowledge and experience, and it is few in number, personal, slow and shaped by reflection. He argues it cannot be assessed as right or wrong or placed on a Beginning to Mastering scale, only judged by the seriousness of the reflection behind it. Using examples such as Andras Schiff, scientists' breakthroughs on walks, Mandela and wine making, he shows why dream time matters. For teachers the implication is that they can tell facts and coach skills but can only facilitate understanding by creating space and time. He ends by warning that over-scheduling children teaches them that being busy beats reflection.
points: Understanding is true only to the person holding it, unlike knowledge, which we agree on, and skills, which can be judged against shared rubrics.
It emerges slowly from reflection on accumulated knowledge and skills and keeps changing shape, like a lava lamp or maturing wine.
It cannot be assessed for correctness, but we can judge the seriousness and thoroughness of the reflection behind it.
Breakthroughs often arrive during dream time away from the working context, so non-contextual space can be valuable.
Teachers and parents can facilitate understanding by protecting reflection time, whereas a packed schedule teaches children that busyness beats reflection.
quotes: But Understanding isn’t true like knowledge or even sort of true like skills.

Understanding is what happens when we reflect on the continual use and repetition of our knowledge and skills in action over time and through our lives. When that reflective simmering happens, something different, something deeper emerges that becomes the bedrock of who we are and how we see the world.

Understanding is impossible to assess because it doesn’t (and shouldn’t) be agreed by everyone, it takes place over time, involves many different disciplines and has a significant personal, reflective element to it.

What makes one person’s ‘understanding’ is the quality of the reflection that has taken place. It’s that quality and seriousness of the reflection that enables us to trust the authenticity of the understanding more than we might otherwise, especially as we might not share it.
Knowledge and skills matter hugely in this process as they provide the kindling for the fire that burns so that reflection can happen.
Teachers, parents and others can't be tellers or coaches of understanding because understanding doesn’t work like that. They are, though, the vital facilitators of it.
By the time they have a pre-frontal cortex ready to do its thing for them, they have already learned something less helpful; that being busy always beats reflection. It doesn’t and it shouldn’t.
